name: journal-peter-against-paul-at-antioch.json
content:
Paul tells one story about Antioch, and nobody else tells it. In Galatians he says he opposed Peter to his face. Acts never mentions it. And Paul never says who won.

What Paul says

Paul writes that "when Cephas came to Antioch, I opposed him to his face, because he stood condemned".1 Cephas is Peter. Before certain men came from James, Peter "was eating with the Gentiles". When they arrived "he drew back and separated himself, fearing the circumcision party".2

Paul then reports the speech he made to Peter "before them all": "If you, though a Jew, live like a Gentile and not like a Jew, how can you force the Gentiles to live like Jews?"3 Peter is accused of forcing Gentiles to keep the law, which is the reverse of what the men from James were asking. Paul has turned a question about table fellowship into a charge of coercion.

[paulus_figure name="antakya-antioch"]Antakya in Turkey, on the site of ancient Antioch in Syria, where Paul says he opposed Cephas to his face (Galatians 2:11).[/paulus_figure]

Who sided with whom

Count the parties. Peter drew back. The men from James came and Peter feared them. "The rest of the Jews acted hypocritically along with him, so that even Barnabas was led astray by their hypocrisy."4 Barnabas had travelled with Paul for years and had been given the same right hand of fellowship by James, Cephas and John.5

Every party Paul names took the other side: Peter, Barnabas, the Jewish believers of Antioch and the delegation from James. He calls all of them hypocrites. They are the people who knew ʿĪsā, or were sent by his brother, or had stood beside Paul at the Jerusalem agreement. [paulus_link slug="james-the-brother" /] and [paulus_link slug="paul-against-the-disciples" /] set out where each of them stood.

Where the story stops

Paul reports his own speech and no reply. He does not write that Peter agreed, or that Barnabas came back, or that the men from James withdrew. A man who had won the argument would say so, and Paul had every reason to, since he wrote Galatians to win the same argument with the Galatians.

Acts does not help. It skips the episode. What it does record is that "there arose a sharp disagreement, so that they separated from each other", and that "Paul chose Silas and departed".6 Luke gives the quarrel over John Mark as the cause of the break with Barnabas. Paul says Barnabas was led astray by Peter's party. One of the two accounts is incomplete, and [paulus_link slug="the-parting-with-barnabas" /] goes through what each leaves out.

A Muslim reading

In the Islamic account ʿĪsā and his disciples lived by the law of Mūsā. Acts agrees about the Jerusalem community: its elders tell Paul that the believers there are "all zealous for the law".7 At Antioch the men closest to ʿĪsā wanted the law kept, and the one man who opposed them is the one who never met him.

The verdict

Everyone in the story except Paul sided against him, and he calls them all hypocrites. He reports his speech. He never reports that anyone gave way.

The simplest reading is that Paul lost the argument at Antioch, left with a new companion, and told his side to the Galatians where none of the others could answer. [paulus_link slug="a-self-appointed-apostle" /] asks who gave him the authority to overrule them.

Peter and Paul at Antioch: questions readers ask

Who was Cephas?

Peter. Paul uses the Aramaic name Cephas and the Greek name Peter for the same man in Galatians 2.

Did Paul rebuke Peter?

By his own account, yes, "before them all" (Galatians 2:14). No other source reports it, and Peter's answer is not recorded.

Who were the men from James?

Messengers from the Jerusalem community led by James, the brother of ʿĪsā. Paul calls them "the circumcision party".

What happened to Barnabas?

Paul says he was "led astray" at Antioch. Acts says he and Paul separated after a sharp disagreement over John Mark, and Barnabas sailed away to Cyprus.
